                                   CHRISTINE JUN HAMMOND
                                   CHRISTOFER C. NOLAN
                                   INNA VINOGRADOV


                                   505 Van Ness Avenue
                                   San Francisco, CA 94102

October 21, 2026
                           UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



    San Diego Gas & Electric Company                 Docket No. ER26-3896-000



                                 PROTEST OF
                 THE CALIFORNIA PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION


I.        INTRODUCTION

          Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 (a)(2) of the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 the

California Public Utilities Commission (“CPUC”) protests San Diego Gas & Electric

Company’s (“SDG&E”) filing in Docket Number ER26-3896-000.

          The proposed tariff changes should be denied for two reasons. First, SDG&E’s

request to approve rate design of transmission rates for the retail Medium Commercial

Class is specifically within the state’s exclusive jurisdiction under the Federal Power Act

Sec. 201. 2 Second, SDG&E’s proposed methodology is not consistent with the retail rate

design in CPUC Decision (D). 25-09-006.

          The Commission has determined that “… it is within a state's exclusive

jurisdiction to determine how … FERC-approved rates are collected among the relevant



1
    18 CFR § 385.211, 18 CFR § 385.214.
2
    16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).


                                              1
 retail consumers… states have exclusive jurisdiction over how to allocate the costs of all

Commission-jurisdictional rates (including for energy, capacity, and transmission) among

retail customers, including allocating costs among different classes of retail customers.” 3

       SDG&E must obtain approval of its proposed transmission retail allocation and

rate design from the CPUC before seeking adoption of such changes at FERC.

II.    PROTEST

       A.      Background and Summary

       On September 22, 2025, the CPUC approved D.25-09-006, a decision creating a

retail Medium Commercial Class and approving rate design methodology for retail

distribution rates for San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E). 4

      On September 30, 2026, SDG&E submitted its tariff change filing at FERC, which

includes updated tariff records for Appendix VII and Appendix IX of SDG&E’s FERC

Electric Transmission Owner Tariff, with an effective date of January 1, 2027. SDG&E

requests the following changes:

            • Base Transmission Revenue Requirement (BTRR) and Reliability Services

               (RS) charges applicable to multiple retail customer classes, including a

               newly created Medium Commercial class.




3
 PJM Interconnection, et al. 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 167 (Dec. 18, 2025). (“PJM Co-Location Order”).
4
 D.25-09-006, Decision Adopting Settlement Agreements to Update Marginal Costs, Cost Allocation and
Electric Rate Design for San Diego Gas & Electric Company (September 18, 2025).


                                                 2
              • Transmission rate determination methodologies, including updated

                treatment of historical sales and demand factors when historical usage

                becomes zero, and allocation of BTRR. 5

        B.      Discussion

                1.      Per Federal Power Act Section 201 and FERC
                        precedent, retail cost allocation and retail rate
                        design is subject to State approval.

        SDG&E’s filing seeks approval of assigning RS charges to multiple retail

customer classes and authorization for transmission rate determination methodologies for

the newly created retail Medium Commercial Class. Both are designs of retail

transmission rates subject to the state’s exclusive jurisdiction.

        The Commission has recently explained the Federal Power Act’s (“FPA”)

jurisdictional division of responsibilities in retail vs. wholesale ratemaking and rate

design. In considering the careful balance that the FPA strikes between state and federal

powers, the Commission determined that states retain exclusive authority over the

specific terms of retail sales and retail rate design. 6 As an agency created by the FPA, the

Commission has jurisdiction only over matters that Congress has given it the authority to

regulate. 7 FPA Section 201(b)(1) gives the Commission jurisdiction over the transmission

of electric energy in interstate commerce, the sale of electric energy at wholesale in


5
  San Diego Gas & Electric Company, Docket No. ER26-3896, Transmission Owner Tariff Revisions to
Appendices VII and IX. (“SDG&E Filing”) Transmittal Letter at 1.
6
  PJM Co-Location Order at P 165.
7
  PJM Co-Location Order at P 166, citing Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 8 (D.C. Cir. 2002).
(“As a federal agency, FERC is a ‘creature of statute,’ having ‘no constitutional or common law existence
or authority, but only those authorities conferred upon it by Congress.’” (emphasis in the original.))


                                                    3
 interstate commerce, and all facilities for such transmission or sale of electric energy. 8

The FPA reserves to the states authority over any matters not expressly conveyed to the

Commission, which includes retail sales and wholesale sales not in interstate commerce,

as well as the facilities used for the generation and distribution of electricity, 9 except as

where otherwise provided. 10 The Supreme Court has long held regulation of these matters

to be within the states' historical police powers, and the Court has observed that the FPA's

jurisdictional divide “was drawn with meticulous regard for the continued exercise of

state power, not to handicap or dilute it in any way.” 11


        Following the FPA’s division of powers in practical application, first, the

Commission approves the overall costs that go into the transmission revenue requirement

and divides the costs between retail and wholesale customers. 12 Second, the State

determines retail customer classes and how the total transmission costs assigned to the

retail customers are allocated among those customer classes. 13 Allocation of RS charges

among retail customers and approval of rate determination methodologies requested by

SDG&E falls squarely within the second step, and is therefore subject to state

jurisdiction.




8
  Id., citing 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).
9
  Id., citing Nat'l Ass'n of Regul. Util. Comm'rs v. FERC, 964 F.3d at 1187 (citing N. Nat. Gas Co. v. State
Corp. Comm'n of the State of Kan., 372 U.S. 84, 91-93 (1963)).
10
   Id., citing 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1); see Dayton Power & Light Co. v. FERC, 126 F.4th 1107, 1129 (6th
Cir. 2025).
11
   PJM Co-Location Order.
12
   PJM Interconnection Show Cause Order, 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 at P 67-68 (Feb. 20, 2025).
13
   Id.


                                                     4
         Finally, the Commission’s recent Show Cause Order (“Order”) to the California

Independent System Operator (CAISO) and the California transmission owners (FERC

Docket No. EL26-71) further supports the CPUC’s position. In the Order, the

Commission made it clear that the states have jurisdiction over retail cost allocation and

retail rate design, and that transmission providers must coordinate with states when

customer-facing rate structures are affected. 14

        2. SDG&E’s proposed methodology has not been reviewed by the CPUC and
        if approved would result in contradictory distribution and transmission retail
        rate designs.
        SDG&E’s filing states that its approach is consistent with CPUC’s rate design. 15

While CPUC D.25-09-006 did create a new retail Medium Commercial Class, 16 the

methodologies proposed by SDG&E in its filing at FERC are problematic for two

reasons: (1) they have not been reviewed or approved by the CPUC, and (2) they would

result in contradictory distribution and transmission retail rate designs if approved by the

Commission.

        The following retail transmission rate methodology proposals from SDG&E’s

filing have not been reviewed and approved by the CPUC:

             • A 25% flat volumetric / 75% demand structure;



14
   California Independent System Operator (CAISO), et al., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the
Federal Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,214 at P 93. (“CAISO OSC” or “Order to Show”).
15
   Transmittal Letter at 2. “Consistent with the approved CPUC-jurisdictional distribution design and reflecting the
mixed nature of customers in the Medium Commercial class, SDG&E is proposing a rate design that recovers costs
using a blended volumetric and demand design, along with a completely volumetric rate for specific schedules.
Approving this filing will create consistency for SDG&E’s customers between their FERC and CPUC-jurisdictional
rates.”
16
   D.25-09-006 at 40-42.


                                                         5
             • A 90% / 10% non-coincident peak charge vs. on-peak demand charge split;

            • A kWh-only allocation for certain Medium Commercial schedules; and

            • Reclassification of EV-HP customers into Medium Commercial for

                transmission purposes. 17

        Separately, D.25-09-006 did not address transmission rate design; 18 however,

SDG&E’s proposed methodology has implications for price signals at both the

distribution and transmission levels. The CPUC-approved distribution design for the

Medium Commercial Class is to recover 65% of demand-related distribution costs via

on-peak demand charges. 19 In contrast, SDG&E’s filing here places only 7.5% of

Medium Commercial transmission revenue in a coincident peak (CP) demand charge

(10% of the 75% of revenues to be collected via the demand structure). 20 If approved, this

would result in a material inconsistency between distribution and transmission rate

designs. In other words, this would create highly asymmetric and conflicting price signals

at the distribution and transmission levels. Furthermore, this undermines CPUC’s retail

rate design principles and customer expectations by substantially understating peak

transmission costs.




17
   Transmittal Letter at 2-4.
18
   See D.25-09-006 generally, e.g. at 86 Conclusion of Law (“COL”) 11, at 87 COL 18.
19
   D.25-09-006 at 36.
20
   See SDG&E Filing, Appendix: “Appendix IX, Determination of SDG&E’s end use customer class
transmission charges, low voltage access charge, and high voltage utility-specific rate, and allocation of
BTRR applicable to high voltage and low voltage transmission facilities.”



                                                     6
        In closing, SDG&E must first file an application for retail rate design at the

CPUC, after which SDG&E’s transmission tariffs can be conformed to reflect the

authorized Medium Commercial Class rate design.

III.   CONCLUSION
       For the reasons discussed above, SDG&E’s tariff changes should be rejected.
